Speciesism
s: Discrimination against those who do not belong to a certain species: giving less weight (or none) to harms and benefits just because of the species of whoever receives them.

t: Anthropocentrism
s: A form of speciesism that puts humans at the center: only humans would matter in themselves, or they would matter more.

t: Sentience
s: The capacity to have positive and negative experiences, such as suffering and enjoyment. A sentient being can be harmed and benefited.

t: Moral consideration
s: Taking into account, in our decisions, someone's good for their own sake, and not only because of the effects on others.

t: Equal consideration
s: The principle that harms and benefits of the same size should have the same weight, whatever the species, race or gender of whoever receives them.

t: Moral agent
s: Someone who can be held responsible for what they do, because they understand moral reasons. Babies and animals are not moral agents.

t: Moral patient
s: Someone who can be morally affected by other people's decisions and therefore must be taken into account. A moral patient does not need to be a moral agent.

t: Moral status
s: The degree of moral importance given to someone. The special status thesis says some individuals have priority even when they suffer less.

t: Veganism
s: The position of not taking part in animal exploitation, refusing products and services that depend on it, as far as possible.

t: Animal exploitation
s: Using animals as resources: for food, clothing, testing, entertainment, labor or companionship.

t: Argument from species overlap
s: If lacking certain capacities does not justify treating some humans worse, then lacking them does not justify treating animals worse either. Also called the argument from marginal cases.

t: Argument from relevance
s: What matters for moral consideration is being able to be harmed or benefited; that depends on sentience, not on species or intelligence.

t: Impartiality test
s: Asking what we would choose if we did not know which position we would occupy among those affected, including which species we would be.

t: Veil of ignorance
s: A device from Rawls: choosing principles without knowing who we will be in society. Applied to animal ethics, without even knowing our species.

t: Benefit of the doubt
s: When we are unsure whether a being is sentient, we should err on the side of caution: the mistake of treating it as an object costs more than the opposite mistake.

t: Magnitude Thesis
s: The strength of our reasons to avoid harming someone and to benefit them depends on the size of the harm or benefit, not on species.

t: Special Status Thesis
s: The idea that some individuals have a "trump card," usually called dignity, that gives them priority even when they would be harmed less.

t: Appeal to nature
s: Arguing that something is right because it is natural. Something being natural does not mean it is good or just.

t: Appeal to tradition
s: Arguing that something is right because it has always been done. Many traditions have been unjust.

t: Appeal to authority
s: Accepting a conclusion because someone important defended it, instead of evaluating the reasons offered.

t: Euthyphro dilemma
s: Is something good because an authority approves of it, or does the authority approve of it because it is good? If the second, what matters is the reasons, not the authority.

t: Metaethics
s: The field that studies the nature of moral judgments: whether there are moral truths, whether they are objective, how we know them.

t: Harm of death
s: The harm that death does to the one who dies. The most widely accepted view: death deprives the individual of the good things they would have lived.

t: Epicurean view of death
s: Epicurus's idea that death is not a harm, because when it comes the individual no longer exists to be harmed.

t: Deprivation
s: An explanation of the harm of death: it prevents (deprives) the individual from having the positive experiences they would have had.

t: QALY
s: Quality-adjusted life year: measures how much lifetime someone loses and how good that time would have been. Used in public health.

t: Psychological connectedness
s: How much someone keeps of their memories, intentions and desires between two moments. Some views say death harms less those who have little connectedness.

t: Replaceability
s: The idea that killing an animal is not wrong if another one is brought into existence in its place. The collection shows why this idea fails.

t: Environmentalism
s: In this collection: views that give intrinsic value to nonsentient entities, such as species and ecosystems, even when that is worse for sentient beings.

t: Holism
s: A view that values the whole (species, ecosystem, biotic community) rather than the individuals that make it up.

t: Biocentrism
s: The view that every living being, sentient or not, deserves moral consideration.

t: Ecocentrism
s: The view that ecosystems and nature as a whole have moral value of their own.

t: Ecological balance
s: The relative stability of population sizes over time. It does not, by itself, show that the animals are doing well.

t: Biodiversity
s: The variety of species in a place. It is a measure of species, not of the well-being of individuals.

t: Intrinsic value
s: The value something has as an end, in itself, and not as a means to something else (instrumental value).

t: Instrumental value
s: The value something has as a means of achieving something else that is valued.

t: Intelligentism
s: Discrimination based on degree of intelligence: giving more weight to those who are more cognitively complex.

t: Valence
s: The positive or negative character of an experience: what makes something feel good or bad.

t: Natural harms
s: Harms that animals suffer from natural processes, such as hunger, disease, parasitism, cold and disasters.

t: Wild animals
s: Animals that live in the wild, outside direct human control. They are the vast majority of sentient beings.

t: r-selection
s: Reproducing by having huge numbers of offspring, almost all of whom die young. It is the rule among animals and explains why suffering prevails in nature.

t: Welfare biology
s: A proposed field of research to study animals in their environments from the point of view of what affects them positively or negatively.

t: Primary productivity
s: The amount of biomass produced by plants in an environment. Reducing it tends to reduce the number of animals born to suffer.

t: Predation
s: One animal hunting and eating another. The collection discusses whether and when we would have reasons to intervene.

t: Altruistic killing
s: A proposal to destroy habitats so that fewer animals are born and suffer. It is debated among advocates for wild animals themselves.

t: Paternalism
s: Acting for someone's good against what they prefer.

t: S-risks
s: Risks that suffering will occur in the future on a gigantic scale, greater than all the suffering that has existed on Earth so far.

t: X-risks
s: Existential risks: risks of the annihilation of humanity or the permanent loss of its potential.

t: Longtermism
s: The position that positively influencing the long-term future is a moral priority.

t: Temporal impartiality
s: Giving the same weight to suffering no matter when it happens: today, a hundred years from now or a million years from now.

t: Expected value
s: The severity of a scenario multiplied by the probability that it will happen. For bad scenarios, we speak of expected disvalue.

t: Substratism
s: Discrimination based on the material a body is made of (organic or not). Carbonism is its form directed against nonorganic beings.

t: Risk factor
s: Something that is not a catastrophe in itself but greatly increases its chance or severity, as in medicine.

t: Broad and targeted strategies
s: Broad strategies try to have a good impact in almost every scenario; targeted ones bet on specific scenarios.

t: Influence triad
s: The three factors that determine an agent's impact on sentient beings: their intentions, their knowledge and their power.

t: Tractability
s: How much of a problem can be solved with the resources available.

t: Neglectedness (criterion)
s: The fewer people are already working on a problem, the more difference each additional person makes.

t: Welfarism
s: An ambiguous term that can name anyone from those who accept exploiting animals "without cruelty" to those who defend reforms as a path to abolition.

t: Abolitionism
s: Advocating an end to animal exploitation, and not merely its regulation.

t: Cultivated meat
s: Meat produced from cultivated cells, without raising and slaughtering animals.

t: Indirect arguments
s: Advocating an end to consuming animals for the sake of health or the environment, rather than because of the harm done to the animals themselves.

t: Total and sufficient approaches
s: The total approach defends a complete ethical view; the sufficient approach shows that certain goals can be accepted from many different views.

t: Shifting the focus
s: Taking speciesism out of the center of the debate by discussing only health, the environment or practical details.

t: Disguised normative objection
s: A disagreement about goals presented as if it were only a strategic doubt ("that would be great, but it won't work").

t: Burden of proof
s: The obligation to justify a claim. Whoever defends harming someone needs to justify the harm.

t: Cognitive bias
s: A systematic distortion in the way we judge, which leads us to wrong conclusions without our noticing.

t: Scope neglect
s: Failing to adjust our concern to the size of a problem: we react almost the same way to a thousand or a million victims.

t: Identifiable victim effect
s: The tendency to help one victim with a face and a name more than many anonymous victims.

t: Status quo bias
s: Preferring things the way they already are, just because they are that way.

t: Motivated reasoning
s: Evaluating arguments more strictly when they go against what we want to believe, and less strictly when they favor us.

t: Moral licensing
s: Feeling entitled to act badly after having done something good. Also called the moral credential effect.

t: Normative ethics
s: The field that investigates what we ought to do and why: which actions are right or wrong.

t: Consequentialism
s: A family of theories whose focal point is consequences: the right thing is whatever produces the best results.

t: Utilitarianism
s: A form of consequentialism that seeks to maximize the total well-being of those affected.

t: Deontology
s: A family of theories whose focal point is rules or duties, which hold even when breaking them would bring better results.

t: Virtue ethics
s: Theories whose focal point is character: the right thing is what a virtuous person would do.

t: Ethics of care
s: A theory centered on relationships and on attention to the concrete needs of the vulnerable.

t: Contractualism
s: Theories according to which morality is whatever would be agreed upon by the parties under suitable conditions.

t: Discourse ethics
s: The theory that valid norms are those that everyone affected would accept in a free dialogue.

t: Prioritarianism
s: Benefits count more the worse off the one who receives them is.

t: Egalitarianism
s: Theories that place value on reducing inequalities between individuals.

t: Sufficientarianism
s: What matters most is that everyone reaches a sufficient level of well-being.

t: Maximin
s: The rule of choosing the option whose worst outcome is the best: giving maximum priority to those who are worst off.

t: Negative utilitarianism
s: A version of utilitarianism that gives priority to reducing suffering over increasing happiness.

t: Theories of well-being
s: They investigate what makes someone's life go well: pleasure (hedonism), the satisfaction of desires, or a list of objective goods.

t: Hedonism
s: The theory that well-being consists of positive experiences and the absence of negative ones.

t: Focal point
s: What each family of theories considers most fundamental: consequences, rules or character traits.

t: Incommensurability
s: When two values cannot be measured on a common scale.

t: Pluralism
s: Views that recognize more than one valuable aspect, which must be weighed against one another.

t: Immanuel Kant
s: German philosopher (1724–1804), author of the ethics of the categorical imperative.
